node.label: Jean Barman
node.date_label: Growing Up British (1984) · The West Beyond the West (1991; third edition 2007) · “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98) · French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women (2014)
node.description: Jean Barman’s The West Beyond the West (1991; third edition 2007) offered an inclusive synthesis of British Columbia’s history. Chris Arnett (2021) describes it as replacing Margaret Ormsby’s Eurocentric 1958 survey with a history in which more people could recognize their place. R. Scott Sheffield (2022) praised the survey but found its Second World War coverage brief and its conclusions about the war’s impact necessarily general. In French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women in the Making of the Pacific Northwest (2014), Barman argues that French Canadian fur-trade workers and the Indigenous women in their lives helped shape the region across the later Canada–United States border, challenging narratives written from the perspectives of those in charge. Heather Devine praised its integration of statistics and individual stories in her BC Studies review (2015/16). “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98) examines how colonial power sexualized Indigenous women’s agency, and criticizes even valued histories for treating male sources and subjects as the whole story. Her earlier educational history studied private schooling and racial inequality in education.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Growing Up British in British Columbia: Boys in Private School (1984); Indian Education in Canada, vol. 1: The Legacy (coedited with Yvonne Hébert and Don McCaskill, 1986); The West Beyond the West (1991; revised 1996; third edition 2007); “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98); French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women in the Making of the Pacific Northwest (2014); On the Cusp of Contact (2020), essays edited by Margery Fee.
node.scope_note: Read the 2014 book’s introduction (pp. 3–9), selected opening and concluding passages of “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality,” named reviews and institutional/publisher pages. The monographs, most middle case studies, Greer’s original, Stoler and Cooper’s original, the 1987 bibliography, joint editorial and 2025 tribute essays remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women (2014), Barman invokes Greer’s warning against losing human complexity in statistics to explain her combination of counting and narrative.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, printed p. 7, “Approach,” paragraph beginning “The three sections”: names Greer on the 1837 rebellion and warns against slighting “that which is not measurable.” Greer’s original and the omitted endnote 7 are unread; no particular Greer title or comprehensive methodological descent asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98), Barman praises Harris’s The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997) while criticizing its male-centred sources, subjects and interpretation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 238, main argument and note 4: Harris is among her “three best books,” each nonetheless “driven by a male perspective.” This is qualified criticism, not rejection; Harris’s book unread for this packet.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98), Barman uses Stoler’s account of colonial regulation of intimacy from the jointly written introduction to Tensions of Empire (1997).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 239–240, notes 7 and 12. Note 12 credits the introduction jointly to Ann Laura Stoler and Frederick Cooper, then explicitly assigns this insight to Stoler’s research in colonial Asia. Note 7 also recommends Race and the Education of Desire (1995). Originals unread; shared authorship is preserved rather than transferring the entire joint essay to Stoler.

proposed_edges.relationship: As coeditors of BC Studies from about 1995, Barman and Harris produced its special double issue Native Peoples and Colonialism (1997/98).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Gavin Wilson, UBC Reports, 19 March 1998, “Special BC Studies issue devoted to First Nations”, https://archive.news.ubc.ca/ubcreports/1998/98mar19/bcstudy.html, paragraph identifying Barman as sharing editing duties with Cole Harris and final substantive paragraph dating their editorship to two and a half years earlier. Journal issue record https://bcstudies.ubc.ca/issue-single/bc-studies-no-115-116-autumn-winter-1997/ confirms no. 115–116, Autumn–Winter 1997, and the special-issue title. Accessibility language removed from the relationship because it concerns the journal’s editorial policy. Task M requires every undirected edge to use relationship_kind comparison, so the existing undirected classification is retained; relation_predicate co_edited and the sentence identify the collaboration. Do not introduce an unsupported co_editing kind or an arrow between coeditors.

proposed_edges.relationship: The West Beyond the West (1991; revised 1996; third edition 2007) offered an inclusive synthesis of British Columbia history that brought overlooked historical actors into the provincial narrative.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UBC Green College interview/report, “A new perspective on British Columbia’s history,” identifies the 1991 synthesis and its standing; Arnett’s review (2021), opening three paragraphs, describes its inclusiveness. Edition dates checked on UBC Press’s French Canadians author biography. Existing regional roster row is preserved. Book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98), Barman argues that colonial power sexualized Indigenous women’s agency, narrowing how their actions could be understood.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 238–241 set out the analytical shift to women; p. 264’s concluding argument explicitly makes agency, not just individual women, the object of sexualization. Opening and conclusion read; middle cases not systematically read. No community narrative or narrator quotation reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: Growing Up British in British Columbia: Boys in Private School (1984) studied the appeal of British schooling and its effects on the province’s social fabric.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher synopsis and contents read; institutional interview’s “Research and resistance” section identifies the dissertation-to-book trajectory. Publisher bibliography indexed record supplies original 1984; current ebook date 2007 is not substituted. Claim is limited to the documented research question; book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women (2014) argues that French Canadian fur-trade workers, together with the Indigenous women in their lives, shaped the Pacific Northwest, and calls for moving beyond narratives written from the perspectives of those in charge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample introduction, pp. 3–4 and 6–9, read. The relationship states Barman’s historiographical intervention; later chapters and family appendix unread. It does not endorse a racial definition of Métis identity or reproduce family histories.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her BC Studies review (2006/07) of Birthright, Adele Perry praises Jean Barman’s introduction to the published play (2005) for giving readers interpretive guidance for examining its representations of interracial intimacy.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the journal’s own website (HTTP 200). Perry discusses Barman’s contextual introduction and earlier Skinner biography. Her criticism of unmarked alterations is explicitly directed at Joan Bryans’ adaptation; it is not attributed to Barman. This edge records the substantive review of Barman’s introduction, without inferring influence on Perry’s research. The 2005 publication year is confirmed in Barman’s own bibliography accompanying her Dictionary of Canadian Biography entry. The play and introduction themselves were not read. The web posting date (2013) is distinct from the review’s issue date (2006/07).
proposed_edges.map_label: Perry reviews Barman’s introduction to Birthright

proposed_edges.relationship: In her BC Studies review (2006/07), Jennifer S. H. Brown praises Jean Barman and Bruce McIntyre Watson’s Leaving Paradise: Indigenous Hawaiians in the Pacific Northwest, 1787–1898 (2006) for organizing fragmentary evidence into an insightful narrative and making the scale and dynamics of Hawaiian presence in the region comprehensible.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the journal’s own website (HTTP 200). The reviewer is credited there as Jennifer Brown. She evaluates the coauthored book’s narrative, comparative treatment of the border, and biographical research. This is a favourable substantive review, represented as an undirected comparison; it does not establish that Brown adopted the book in her own subsequent research. The publisher’s hardback listing confirms May 2006; the later paperback is dated December 2021. The book itself was not read. The web posting date (2013) is distinct from the review’s issue date (2006/07).
